open-question.question: Which of the historical cases whose alternative set missed the direction the answer took does the one-off check re-run: every case rated a strong candidate, or a smaller fixed subset?
open-question.recommendation: The list was judged and fixed before any new wording existed, so no case is chosen after the fact, and twenty cases are the smallest set on which a comparison between two rule versions is more than anecdote; the unrated premise cases would add noisier verdicts than evidence.
open-question.alternative: Re-run all 20 historical cases already rated strong candidates for a re-run (16 where the answer took a direction no option represented, 4 where it took a combination on an axis the set never laid out), and add no others. It reuses the already-judged, fixed list, so no case is selected after the new wording exists. Twenty cases are also enough for a share-based pass bar to mean something. It costs twenty grounded runs, and each one needs its own historical project state, however the run-location question settles. The list also holds no case where the answer rejected a premise every option shared, so any premise-related wording gets no evidence from it.

Re-run a smaller subset of the 20 strong candidates, fixed before the enumeration wording is rewritten and drawn in proportion to their mix of coverage gaps and uncrossed-axis combinations. It is the cheapest option in runs, historical checkouts, and the user's time spent reviewing the re-run sets, and fixing it in advance still guards against picking cases the new wording happens to fix. A handful of cases makes any share-based bar coarse, with each case swinging the result by a large step. Only a few combination cases can appear, and premise-shift cases are still absent.

Re-run every historical case whose set missed the direction the answer took, whatever its rating: all 41 (20 coverage gaps, 12 uncrossed-axis combinations, 9 shared-premise rejections). It gives the broadest evidence and is the only option that tests all three missed-direction patterns in full, including the shared-premise pattern the strong-candidate list lacks. It costs about twice the runs and grounding work. The lower-rated cases were judged weaker benchmark material, so they add verdicts that are noisier and harder to judge, which weighs more if a person rather than the agent does the judging.

Re-run a fixed subset chosen before the rewrite to span every missed-direction pattern: a few strong coverage-gap cases, a few strong combination cases, and a few shared-premise cases taken from outside the strong list. Each generic failure pattern the new rules target gets at least some evidence, for far less than re-running every missed case. Each pattern gets only a few cases, so a per-pattern result is anecdotal. The shared-premise cases were never rated strong, so their verdicts rest on weaker material than the rest of the sample.

open-question.question: Does the one-off check also re-run control cases, where the historical alternative set already contained the direction the answer took, to see that the new rules neither lose that direction nor pad the set?
open-question.recommendation: Dropping the count guideline and adding a drop-it check make padding the change's main regression risk, which missed-direction cases cannot show; a small fixed sample of sets already complete on direction shows it directly and reuses verdicts the benchmark material already holds.
open-question.alternative: The check also re-runs a small fixed sample of the refinement overrides. These are the manual answers (65 of the 106 overrides) that refined an option the historical set already listed. For each, it checks that the re-run set still holds that option's direction and has no near-duplicate or filler options. These cases are closest to the candidates: the same answer path, judged by the same verdicts already in the benchmark material. They show directly whether a set that was already covering stays covering. And because refinement means the historical set was complete on direction, extra options there are a clear sign of padding. It adds re-runs and a second matching judgment. A refinement answer often changes the option's details, so judging whether the re-run holds "the same direction" is fuzzier than for a set-chosen answer. The sample also draws only from cases where the user overrode the set, so the far larger mass of accepted picks goes untested.

The one-off check re-runs only the cases whose historical set missed the answer's direction. Loss of a direction and padding are judged by reading the re-run candidate sets and the rewritten wording, and a proper regression side is left to the benchmark-harness idea document under temp/. This is the smallest and cheapest check. Every re-run goes to the failure the milestone exists to fix, and it adds no case selection or matching work beyond what the candidate cases already need. It cannot show that the new rules keep a direction the old rules already found. It also cannot tell growth the rules call for from padding, because every re-run case is one where the historical set was known to be incomplete. So a regression on the most common kind of question, where the set was already right, would go unseen until later milestones.

The check also re-runs a small fixed sample of questions answered by a listed option unchanged. These are Recommendation-answer or Alternative-answer commits. For each, it checks that the re-run set still holds the chosen option's direction and has not grown with padding. These cases stand for how the pass is normally used: the great majority of recorded answers take an embedded option as it is. The direction to match is exactly one historical alternative, so the "still contains it" judgment is as clean as the check can get. No judged verdicts exist yet for these commits, so selecting the sample is new work, done by hand. And an accepted recommendation shows only that the user found the set good enough, not that it was complete, which makes it a weaker baseline for telling growth the rules call for from padding.

The check re-runs control cases from both pools: some refinement overrides and some set-chosen answers. Each is checked for keeping the chosen direction and for not padding the set. This covers both kinds of regression risk, the overridden-but-covered set and the routine accepted set. So a "no loss, no padding" result says something about the pass as a whole, not about one slice of it. It is the costliest control design: the most re-runs, two ways of selecting cases, and two kinds of matching judgment, all for a one-off check. It also increases the privacy-safe aggregate reporting the milestone must commit, and it duplicates much of what the planned benchmark harness would do systematically.

open-question.question: Does the one-off check also run the unchanged enumeration rules on the same cases with the same model, so that a difference in the result can be attributed to the new wording and not to the model?
open-question.recommendation: One extra run per case is the cheapest design that separates the wording's effect from the model's and that can also show a case where the new rules lose a direction the old ones find, which the recovered-only baseline never can; repeated runs exceed a one-off check.
open-question.alternative: Run the unchanged `alternatives-procedure.md`, taken from the commit before the rewrite, once on every re-run case with the same model and effort setting as the new-rules run. Compare each case's two sets side by side. Separates the wording's effect from the model's for every case, and costs only one extra run per case. It also shows where the old rules already recover the missing direction with today's model, and where the new rules lose something the old ones found. Doubles the cost of the check and needs the pre-change procedure runnable in the same grounded setting. With a single sample per arm, one lucky or unlucky run can still create or hide a difference, so the attribution holds only for a clear margin. How the pairs are counted also depends on how the pass bar is expressed.

Run only the rewritten enumeration rules over the chosen cases, and judge each new set against the historical set already on record in the benchmark material, with no fresh run of the unchanged rules. Cheapest and simplest form of the check: it needs half the runs, and there is no need to make the pre-change procedure loadable next to the rebuilt `hosts/claude` tree that the maintainer's install points at. The historical sets came from older models, efforts and procedure versions, often grounded in a different project state. A recovered direction could therefore be the model's doing rather than the new wording's, so the check cannot show that the rewrite caused an improvement. At most it can note this as a caveat.

Run both the unchanged and the rewritten rules several times per case with the same model and effort setting, and compare how often each arm's sets contain the previously missing direction. Controls for the model's run-to-run variation as well as the model itself. A difference in hit rate between the arms can be credited to the wording with real confidence. Multiplies the run count and the review load well past a one-off check, since every extra set must be judged for a match. It also turns the result into rates, which the pass bar and whoever judges matches would have to accommodate.

Run the new rules first, then run the unchanged rules with the same model and effort setting only on the cases where the new set recovered the missing direction. The goal is to confirm the old rules would not have recovered it too. Puts the attribution test exactly where a claimed improvement needs it, and costs fewer extra runs than a full paired baseline when the new rules recover only part of the cases. It is lopsided: it never shows cases where the old rules would have done better than the new ones. The cases it baselines are chosen by the new rules' own result, so it can confirm gains but never find losses.

open-question.question: Where does the one-off check run the alternatives pass so that each case is grounded in its historical project state while the repositories the cases come from receive no commits or other changes?
open-question.recommendation: It is the only option that both leaves the source repositories untouched by construction and runs the pass exactly as shipped over a full historical tree, with no ancestor instructions from this repository leaking into the grounding; the explicitly loaded plugin tree also lets the unchanged rules run in the same setting.
open-question.alternative: For each case, clone the source repository into a scratch directory outside this working copy (for example under the system temp directory), check out the parent of the answer commit, and run the alternatives pass there. The clone's rebuilt `hosts/claude` plugin is loaded explicitly, and the clone is deleted once its set has been read. The source repository is only read. Its working tree, refs, and object store never change, and the pass's own `Alternatives-annotation:` commits land in the throwaway clone. The pass runs exactly as shipped, orchestrator included, grounded in a full historical tree with its history, and no ancestor directory adds cairn's own `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/` settings to the grounding context. Every case needs its own clone and checkout, spread over several source repositories, and the scratch location is picked by hand outside the gitignored `temp/`. Answer commits whose parent predates the XML split have no `open_questions.xml`, so the bare block has to be rebuilt inside each clone before the tool will run.

Make the same per-case clone checked out at the answer commit's parent, but place it under this repository's gitignored `temp/` beside the benchmark material, and run the pass inside it. The source repositories are untouched, the pass commits only into its clone, and everything the check produces stays together with the extracted cases and verdicts in one ignored place. That place is already outside every committed artifact, as the privacy requirement demands. A session started inside `temp/<clone>` sits below cairn's working copy, so cairn's `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` directory load as ancestor context. The historical project would be grounded with this repository's invariants mixed in, which can change what the enumerator treats as the project, and cairn's own cases would effectively be seen twice.

Add a detached `git worktree` of each source repository at the answer commit's parent in a scratch directory, run the pass there, then remove the worktree and prune. It is the cheapest way to get a full historical checkout. No objects are copied and creation is near-instant, so re-running many cases, or a baseline beside them, stays fast. A worktree shares the source repository's `.git`. Adding it writes administrative entries there, and the orchestrator's annotation commits become objects and reflog entries in the source's store until they are pruned or garbage-collected. That breaks the requirement that the source repositories receive no commits or other changes, and cleanup has to be trusted rather than being guaranteed by construction.

Export only the parent commit's tree (for example with `git archive`) into a scratch directory outside this working copy, `git init` it with a single snapshot commit so the orchestrator can commit, and run the pass there. The source repository is only read, and the scratch copy carries no history, remote, or refs. It exposes the least private material and cannot pick up the eventual answer from later history. It is also lighter than a full clone when many cases share one large repository. With no history, any grounding that would look at earlier commits or the milestone's own past finds nothing, so the re-run sees a thinner project than the original pass did. The per-case set-up (export, init, commit, rebuilding the bare block) is scripting the check must own.

Materialize no project copy. Place only the rebuilt milestone directory, holding the bare block and the parent's `requirements.md`, in a scratch directory. Dispatch the alternatives subagent directly, with no orchestrator and so no commit, and have it read every other historical file through read-only `git -C <source> show <parent>:<path>`. No clone, worktree, or checkout is made, and nothing commits anywhere. The source repositories are touched only by read-only git plumbing, and set-up per case is just the one milestone directory. It changes the agent's grounding from "read the working tree" to an instructed git-show route, so the check tests a modified procedure rather than the shipped one. An agent that reads the live source tree by habit would see state from after the answer, possibly including the answer itself, which would contaminate the result.

Drop grounding in the historical project. Run the pass in one scratch fixture that holds only a milestone directory per case (the question block with its alternatives stripped, plus the parent's `requirements.md`), so the enumerator reasons from the question and milestone prose alone. It is the simplest and cheapest setup with the strongest isolation. One fixture serves every case, nothing from the source repositories is copied beyond two milestone files, and the orchestrator's commits land only in the fixture. It measures enumeration without the project reading that the procedure's step 1 requires. Missing directions that the real project would have made obvious, such as a section whose facts are already owned elsewhere, may not come up, so a pass or a fail says little about how the shipped pass behaves.

open-question.question: If the one-off check falls short of its bar, does the milestone revise the enumeration wording and re-run the check, or record the shortfall and finish?
open-question.recommendation: A single bounded round makes a real attempt to close a measured gap while guaranteeing the milestone ends, and it limits tuning against the same small case set, which an open-ended loop or a judged out-of-reach exclusion would not.
open-question.alternative: If the check falls short, the milestone revises the wording a fixed small number of times, typically once, and re-runs the check each time. If it still falls short after the last round, it records the aggregate shortfall and finishes with the best wording it has. On the three choices: revise on any shortfall, stop after a set number of rounds, and ship even if the bar is still missed. It makes a real attempt to close the gap while guaranteeing the milestone ends. That avoids both an open-ended tuning loop and giving up after the first try. The number of rounds is arbitrary. The wording that ships may still be unverified, just with one more round of tuning on the same cases, so the overfitting risk stays, only smaller. Each round also costs another full alternatives pass over every case.

If the check falls short, the milestone revises the enumeration wording and re-runs the check as many times as it takes to reach the bar. On the three choices involved, this means: revise on any shortfall, stop only when the bar is met, and ship only a rewrite that passed. The goal says the change "is verified by" the re-run, and this is the only option where that is literally true when the milestone finishes. Whatever wording ships has met the bar. The loop has no bound, so the milestone could stay open indefinitely. Each round tunes the wording against the same historical cases, which risks overfitting to about 20 known misses instead of improving enumeration in general. And if the bar can't be reached at all, for example because some answers depended on information that no grounded project state contains, the loop never ends. How much a re-run shows also depends on how the sibling baseline and control-case questions settle.

The check runs once, and a shortfall does not reopen the rewrite. The milestone records the aggregate result, meaning only the share met with no case detail, since benchmark data can't be committed. It ships the new wording as written and finishes, leaving further improvement to later work such as the benchmark-harness idea document. On the three choices: never revise because of the check, stop after one run, and ship regardless. It keeps the check one-off, as the goal describes it. The result is an honest measurement instead of a number tuned to the cases, and the milestone's scope and length stay predictable. A rewrite that measurably missed its own bar ships anyway, so the bar becomes informational rather than a gate. A known weakness in the wording is left for a milestone that may never be defined.

If the check falls short, the new enumeration rules are not shipped. The milestone keeps or restores the current step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md, records the aggregate shortfall, and finishes. The review skill's authoring change and the two temp/ idea documents can still land. On the three choices: never revise, stop after one run, and ship nothing unless the bar is met. It treats the bar as a real gate. The workflow never runs enumeration rules that failed their own verification, and the current rules, whose behaviour the benchmark already characterises, stay in force. It throws away a rewrite that may still be better than the current rules even though it missed the bar. And a shortfall on the missing-direction measure says nothing about whether the new rules are worse, so a partial gain is discarded along with the miss.

If the check falls short, each case that still lacks the direction is first sorted by cause. Misses the wording could plausibly have prevented trigger a wording revision and a re-run. Misses the pass could not reach from its grounded project state, such as an answer that turned on information outside the repository, are recorded as out of reach and dropped from the shortfall. The milestone then finishes. On the three choices: revise only for misses caused by the wording, stop once none of those remain, and ship the result. It aims the revision effort only at failures the wording can actually fix. This keeps an unreachable case from forcing endless rewording or from counting against a rule that could never have caught it. Classifying a miss as out of reach is a judgment call that can quietly lower the bar. How trustworthy that judgment is depends on how the sibling question about who judges a match settles. The per-case reasoning also has to stay out of every committed artifact, with only its aggregate recorded.

open-question.question: Which documents outside core/ are updated to match the new enumeration and authoring rules, among docs/skill-reference.md, claim 4 of docs/design-claims.md with its count of two to four alternatives, and CLAUDE.md?
open-question.recommendation: The milestone changes what two skills promise, and the skill reference and design claims are where that promise is stated, so correcting only the counts would leave both pages silent on the new behaviour; a brief statement per governed entry follows how earlier milestones aligned these pages, and the unmeasured metric is left alone.
open-question.alternative: skill-reference.md states the new rules briefly in the entries they govern: the enumeration rules in discuss-open-question, provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions and the alternatives subagent, and the one-axis rule in review-milestone-requirements. Claim 4's Design is rewritten to say the alternatives are distinct and cover the decision, with no count. Its Metric line stays as it is. docs/workflow.md and CLAUDE.md are not edited, and the CLAUDE.md invariant entry is left to its sibling question. Both reader-facing references tell the truth about the new behaviour. Someone reading skill-reference.md or the design claims sees what an alternative set now promises and why questions come one axis at a time. The rules then appear in words in both core/shared/alternatives-procedure.md and several skill-reference.md entries. The build's --check does not cover docs/, so a later wording change in core/ can quietly leave the docs behind. Claim 4's metric also still measures a generic quality score rather than coverage.

Only files under core/ and the rebuilt hosts/ trees change. docs/skill-reference.md, docs/design-claims.md, docs/workflow.md and CLAUDE.md stay as they are, and any doc alignment waits for a later milestone. The CLAUDE.md invariant entry is left to the sibling question on the enumeration rationale record. This is the smallest diff. The milestone's effort goes into the procedure wording and its one-off check, and no doc text is fixed before the check shows the new rules work. Two statements become false as soon as the procedure drops its count. The discuss-open-question entry in skill-reference.md promises "2–4 honest alternatives", and claim 4 of design-claims.md says the recommender "gives 2 to 4 real alternatives". The docs would then contradict the runtime, which goes against the project's own one-source-of-truth claim (17).

Only the two sentences that the change makes false are edited. The "2–4 honest alternatives" phrase in the discuss-open-question entry of skill-reference.md and the "2 to 4 real alternatives" phrase in claim 4's Design line both get count-free wording. No other entry, claim or metric changes, and CLAUDE.md is untouched apart from what its sibling question decides. No doc contradicts the runtime anymore, and the edit stays tiny. skill-reference.md stays a description of how skills work rather than a second copy of the enumeration rules, which avoids new drift. A reader of the docs never learns what now makes a set complete (distinct on an axis, covering the underlying decision, not doing it at all where viable). Nor do they learn that review-milestone-requirements now writes each question on a single axis. Claim 4 keeps a metric that does not measure the property the milestone introduces.

This does everything in the previous option and also replaces claim 4's Metric with one that measures the new property. Examples: the share of overriding answers that took a direction no listed option represented, and the number of sets holding near-duplicate options. It is worded generically, with no case data from the benchmark. Claim 4's design and metric then describe the same thing. The metric names exactly what the milestone's one-off check measures, and a future benchmark harness could adopt it. It adds a metric that no suite runs, on a page that already admits nothing tests claim 4. A metric shaped by the private benchmark also risks carrying more than aggregate or generic information into a committed file, which the goal forbids.

This goes beyond the three documents the question names. Every file outside core/ that describes enumeration or question authoring is updated: skill-reference.md and claim 4 as in the options above, plus the paragraph in docs/workflow.md that explains the two annotating passes and the one-line skill entries in CLAUDE.md for review-milestone-requirements and the alternatives pass. The CLAUDE.md invariant entry is still left to its sibling question. It leaves no page describing the old behaviour. workflow.md's account of the enumerate-versus-pick split, and CLAUDE.md's summary of the review skill as sole author, would both mention the new distinct-and-covering and one-axis properties. It is the largest doc diff, and it touches pages that state no count and so are not actually wrong today. The rules end up repeated in four places with no automated check to keep them in step with core/. It also partly overlaps the sibling question on the enumeration rationale record, which decides what CLAUDE.md says about these rules.

open-question.question: Does CLAUDE.md gain an invariant entry explaining why alternative sets must be distinct and covering and why the count guideline is gone, or does the procedure's own wording carry that alone?
open-question.recommendation: A count guideline and a tidy shortlist are the natural reading a later editor would restore when a set grows large, runtime files may not carry that editor-facing reason, and the existing two-halves bullet is about file separation; the entry states the rule and its generic failure patterns without measurement figures.
open-question.alternative: Add a dedicated invariant bullet to CLAUDE.md. It explains why an alternative set must be distinct and covering: every two options differ in substance on an axis, and the set covers the underlying decision, including dropping the thing where that is viable. It also explains why the "two to four" count guideline was removed and must not be restored, why each option states its axis positions, and how the one-axis authoring rule in review-milestone-requirements stops the set from growing. The rationale uses only aggregate findings and generic patterns from the benchmark. This follows the repository's rule that runtime files carry no editor-facing prose and that rationale belongs in CLAUDE.md. It also gives later editors an explicit "do not fix back" guard, so they won't reinstate a count cap or a tidy shortlist when a set grows large. That is exactly the kind of well-meant regression the other invariant entries exist to prevent. It adds another long bullet to a list that is already dense, and its wording has to be kept in step with the procedure text. The benchmark-privacy rule also limits the evidence to aggregates, so the rationale can't point to the concrete cases that motivated it.

Leave the invariant list's structure alone and add a short clause to the existing bullet "The two halves of the analytical core". The clause says that the enumeration half maps the decision space (distinct, covering, no count guideline) and why. The review-side one-axis authoring rule is noted briefly in the "Tidy vs. record" bullet or left out. The rationale sits next to the invariant that already defines the enumeration half's role, so CLAUDE.md gets only a small addition and there is no new top-level entry to keep aligned. That bullet is about why the two halves are separate files, not what makes a set complete, so the new rule sits in a bullet whose heading doesn't point to it and is easy to miss. Splitting the enumeration and authoring rationale across two bullets also hides that they are two halves of one design.

Make no CLAUDE.md change for this rule. The rewritten step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md carries the requirement and the runner-facing reason for it, as it already does for "complete now". The history is left to milestone 38's recorded decisions and commits. There is only one place to maintain, and it is the text the runner actually reads, so rule and reason can't drift apart. It also keeps CLAUDE.md for decisions that are truly structural rather than prose-quality rules. Nothing tells a later editor that removing the count guideline was deliberate. The runtime-prose rule keeps editor-facing rationale such as "do not restore the cap" out of the procedure, so a future cleanup could put "typically two to four" back without anything flagging a regression. Milestone decisions and commit history are not places an editor checks before editing.

Record the rationale in docs/design-claims.md instead of CLAUDE.md. Claim 4, which currently promises "2 to 4 real alternatives", is rewritten to state the distinct-and-covering property and the evidence pattern behind it. CLAUDE.md stays unchanged. Claim 4 has to be corrected anyway because its count is now wrong. Putting the reason where the property is claimed and its metric is named keeps the justification next to the promise it supports, and CLAUDE.md gets no heavier. design-claims.md is aimed at readers evaluating the plugin, not the file a maintainer or agent loads before editing core/. So it doesn't protect against a count cap being reinstated during an edit, which is the job CLAUDE.md's "Rationale lives here" rule assigns. It also overlaps with the separate Documentation scope question.

open-question.question: Does the enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md tell the enumerator to find what the question's wording takes for granted and weigh rejecting it, or is covering the underlying decision stated without such a step?
open-question.recommendation: One mechanism then covers both the axes the question names and the ones its wording hides, a premise-rejecting option states its stance like any other option, and rejecting a premise usually makes the remaining axes moot, so it adds one option rather than a cross-product.
open-question.alternative: Premise-finding is folded into the enumeration's axis work rather than stated as a rule of its own: each assumption the wording takes for granted is treated as one more axis of the decision, with accepting and rejecting it as its values, so rejecting a premise comes out of the same step that lays out the other axes. A single mechanism covers both the axes the question names and the ones its wording hides, so the procedure gains no separate premise rule. A premise-rejecting option then carries its stance on every other axis like any other option, and does not stand outside the set's structure. It only works if the enumeration step contains an explicit axis step, so its viability depends on how the Axis identification step sibling settles. Treating every premise as an axis also multiplies the combinations the goal says must all be weighed, and on a multi-axis question that can make the set grow more than the problem requires.

The enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md gets its own instruction: before listing options, name what the question's wording takes for granted (an assumed need, mechanism, or framing), then for each such premise weigh an option that rejects it, and list that option only where it is honestly viable. On the axes it touches, this option adds a dedicated process step, so a premise is examined on every question and not only when the enumerator happens to notice it. It targets a failure the benchmark aggregate shows directly: 9 of 106 overriding answers rejected a premise that every listed option shared. A named step makes the enumerator look for exactly the assumption that a wording-bound set carries silently, rather than hoping the general coverage requirement brings it up. It lengthens a procedure that every alternatives subagent and discuss-open-question follow on every question, although most questions have no premise worth rejecting. It also invites premise-rejecting options that are really strawmen, which works against the existing ban on padding. How much it overlaps other rules depends on how the Drop-it direction rule and Axis identification step siblings settle, because not doing the thing is itself the rejection of one premise.

The enumeration step says only that the set must cover the underlying decision and not the question's wording, with no step for finding premises. Spotting and rejecting a premise is left to the enumerator's judgment under that one requirement, and premise problems on the authoring side are left to the "shared premises" idea document the milestone writes under temp/. It keeps the procedure short and states the outcome without prescribing a method, the same approach step 2 already takes with "complete now". It adds no rule that could push premise-rejecting options into a set whose premises are sound. The current procedure already asks for completeness without defining it, and the historical sets still missed shared premises. A bare "underlying decision" requirement may be too abstract to change what the enumerator actually does, and nothing points it at the particular assumption every option shares.

There is no process step. Instead, the coverage requirement comes with one concrete test the finished set must pass: if every listed option shares an assumption the question's wording introduced, the set must either include an option that rejects that assumption or leave it out only because rejecting it is not viable in this project. The check sits in step 2 next to the completeness requirement. It aims precisely at the benchmark category, a premise that every option shared, while leaving the enumeration method free. Because the test only fires when all the options agree on an assumption, it adds nothing to sets that already vary on it. Running the test still requires the enumerator to see the shared assumption, which is the step that failed in the historical cases, so it may catch little more than the bare property does. A self-check the finished set must pass is also harder to verify in the one-off re-run than a visible step.

open-question.question: When an axis of the underlying decision is already the subject of a sibling open question, does an alternative set's coverage extend to that axis, or does the existing rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling bound it?
open-question.recommendation: Each axis stays decided in exactly one block, which is what keeps the parallel alternatives pass and the scope-only sibling rule safe, while the required condition in the drawback gives the recommendation pass the cross-question constraint it turns into a dependency; choices coupled tightly enough to need laid-out combinations never reach two blocks.
open-question.alternative: Siblings still bound the set, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis. But the enumeration step now explicitly requires each option to name any sibling-owned axis its viability depends on, stated as a condition in its drawback without naming the expected outcome. This turns today's optional "say so in its drawback" into a required statement. It shows interdependence across questions without duplicating any decision. The recommendation pass gets the constraint in the option text, where it can become a depends-on tag. The block format needs no set-level statement, which the tool would refuse anyway. Unviable pairings are described one option at a time rather than laid out as combinations, so a combination spanning two questions is still never an option anyone can pick. It also adds a duty the enumerator must remember for every option, and the drawback field gets longer.

Keep the existing step-1 rule as the limit on coverage. The set covers only the axes of the underlying decision that no sibling question owns, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis, and each option's what-it-is text states its position only on the axes this question owns. Each axis is decided in exactly one block. This keeps the rule that siblings supply scope and are never assumed settled, which is what lets the alternatives pass annotate blocks in parallel. It also keeps sets small, so one-axis-per-question authoring actually limits growth. Where a sibling-owned axis constrains this one, no set shows which pairings are unviable. The 12 historical overrides that took a combination on an axis the set never laid out could still fall between two questions, because each block's coverage stops at the boundary.

Retire the rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling. Every axis of the underlying decision is laid out and each option states where it stands on it, including axes a sibling question also owns. This is the most literal reading of the goal's "cover the underlying decision" and "every combination weighed" requirements. Each set becomes a complete map of the decision, so an answer taking a cross-question combination can always find it listed. The same axis gets decided in two blocks. Recording one question's answer can fix a stance on a sibling's axis and conflict with that sibling's later answer, which causes more strip-and-re-run cascades. Stating a position on a sibling axis also comes close to presuming how that sibling settles, which step 2 forbids. Sets grow in exactly the way one-axis authoring is meant to prevent.

Siblings bound coverage by default. The one exception is a sibling-owned axis that constrains this question's axis so that not every pairing is viable: then the set lays out the viable combinations across both axes, and each option states its position on both. It targets the missed-combination failure without duplicating independent sibling decisions. Fuller coverage applies only where a single-axis set would really mislead. The enumerator has to judge interdependence per question, a conditional rule that is harder to apply the same way every time. Where it applies, it brings back the double-decided axis and the answer-time conflicts. Its merit turns on how the question of authoring interdependent axes settles, since that question decides whether such pairs reach two blocks in the first place.

open-question.question: Who decides whether a re-run alternative set contains the direction the historical answer took: the agent carrying out the check, or the user reviewing the sets?
open-question.recommendation: With sets from both rule versions to mix, a judge that does not know which version produced a set removes the self-grading bias at no cost in user time, and its verdicts stay comparable across the two arms, which is what the comparison needs.
open-question.alternative: A separate judge agent decides each match. It gets its own context with only the historical answer, the recorded missing direction, and the re-run set, and it is not told which rule version produced the set. The user receives only its verdicts. It removes the self-grading bias of the agent carrying out the check while still asking nothing of the user. Hiding which rules produced each set makes the verdicts comparable across runs. Setting up a separate, blinded judging step adds work to a one-off check. The judge is still a model making a fuzzy call with no human anchor. How much the blinding is worth depends on whether the check also produces sets from the unchanged rules to mix in.

The agent running the check decides each match by comparing the re-run set against the missing direction already recorded for that case in the benchmark's judged verdicts, and hands the user only the tally and a short aggregate summary. It takes the least of the user's time and fits a headless or scripted run. It also reuses the same kind of judgment that produced the 20 strong-candidate ratings, so the check measures against the same yardstick that selected its cases. The agent that wrote or ran the new rules is grading its own work, and "contains the direction" is a fuzzy semantic call. A lenient reading of near-misses could pass the change without anyone catching it, and no human ever sees the sets the verdict rests on.

The agent puts each case in front of the user: the historical question, the direction the answer took, and the re-run set. It gives no verdict of its own, and the user decides for every case whether the set contains that direction. The person whose answers produced the overrides decides whether each missing direction now appears, which is the most faithful reading of what "the direction the answer took" meant. The verdict carries no model bias. It costs the most user time, because every case's set must be read in full. User judgments are harder to repeat identically on a later re-run, and the user may not recall the context behind older answers from other projects.

The agent records a verdict and a one-line reason for every case, and the user reviews and confirms or overturns each one before the tally counts. The user holds the final say on every case at a fraction of the reading cost, since each verdict comes with the specific option the agent believes matches. Overturned verdicts also show where the agent's judgment of a match is unreliable. A proposed verdict anchors the reviewer, so review tends to become rubber-stamping and the human check is weaker than it looks. The user still has to open every case, so the saving over judging every set directly may be small.

The agent decides each match and marks as uncertain any case where the closest option is only near the historical direction. The user adjudicates only the uncertain cases, plus optionally a small spot-check of the confident ones. Human attention goes where the call is actually hard, so the user's time grows with the number of ambiguous cases rather than the number of re-run cases. Clear hits and clear misses pass without review. It relies on the agent to know which of its own calls are doubtful. A confidently wrong verdict escapes review unless a spot-check happens to catch it, so the tally is only partly human-verified.

open-question.question: What share of the re-run cases must contain the previously missing direction for the one-off check to count the change as verified?
open-question.recommendation: The historical sets came from older models, so an absolute share could be met by the model alone; only a margin over the unchanged rules on the same cases credits the result to the wording, with the margin for clearly more fixed before the runs.
open-question.alternative: Set no absolute share. The change counts as verified when the new rules recover the missing direction in clearly more of the same cases than the unchanged rules recover when run with the same model. A pass can be credited to the new wording and not to the model. Newer models may already recover some directions that the historical run missed, and an absolute share cannot separate that effect from the wording change. It only means something if the check also runs the unchanged rules, which the sibling question on a baseline run decides. It doubles the number of runs. With a small number of cases it still needs a stated margin for "clearly more", so the arbitrary cut-off is moved, not removed.

Set a fixed share of more than half: the change counts as verified when most of the re-run cases now contain the direction their historical set missed. The bar is stated as a share, so it applies unchanged whichever set of cases the check re-runs. It is a simple bar that can be failed, and the new rules can reasonably reach it. Some historical misses turned on facts nobody had when the question was asked, so no enumeration rule could recover them. A majority bar leaves room for those cases and still requires the rules to fix the typical miss. The cut-off at one half is arbitrary. The cases are a small, hand-picked set, not a random sample, so a single case can move the result across the line, and the verdict says little about how the rules perform on new questions.

Set a fixed share well above half, around three quarters or more: the change counts as verified only when nearly every re-run case now contains the direction its historical set missed. Passing it is strong evidence that the rewritten enumeration step does what the goal claims, which is to cover the underlying decision, including the direction of not doing the thing. A borderline improvement cannot be reported as success. Some misses may not be recoverable by any enumeration rule, so a failure can reflect the chosen cases rather than the wording. That makes a shortfall more likely, and what happens then depends on how the sibling question on shortfall response settles.

Apply a share bar separately to each kind of historical miss: a direction no option represented, a combination on an axis the set never laid out, and a premise every option shared. The change counts as verified only when each kind meets its bar. Each new rule is checked on its own. A pass driven only by the frequent "not doing the thing" misses cannot hide that the rules on combinations or premises had no effect. Split across three kinds, each group holds only a few cases, so each share is very noisy. Every case also needs a category label, which is extra judging work on data that must stay outside the repository.

Set no pass share. The check re-runs the cases, records the aggregate share that now contains the missing direction, and the user decides from that result whether the change is verified. It does not claim statistical meaning for a threshold chosen in advance on a small, non-random set of cases. This suits a check that runs once and whose committed trace is limited to aggregate results by the milestone's privacy rule. The check can no longer fail by a stated rule, so "verified" becomes a judgment made after seeing the result. It also gives the sibling question on shortfall response no defined trigger to act on.
